title: The many faces of Belobog
description: From Slavic transcription to Unicode: why Belobog is more than a domain name.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# The many faces of Belobog

No important name has only one face. **Belobog** appears as a ​figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the ‌name and its roots, the Slavic transcription original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. ‌Taken together, those faces explain why *belobog* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Belobog
- **ASCII ​form:** belobog
- **Meaning:** "White god"
- **Domain of influence:** Light, Good, Fortune
- **Pantheon:** Slavic
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Belobog** (*belobog*) — Light, Good, Fortune · White god — belongs to the Slavic tradition, where ​it is catalogued under the domain "Light, Good, Fortune". The name means "White god".

**Belobog** is light, good, fortune. The name means "White god" and belongs to the slavic tradition.

PuniCodex restores the ​name as **Belobog** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/belobog/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The plain ASCII form *belobog* survives as a modern convenience ​imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Belobog** is a scholarly ​transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "White god".

The ASCII form *belobog* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not ‌an ancient spelling. No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual slavic names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

The form **Belobog** is ‌therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

The restoration Belobog keeps the prosodic information visible even when the ‌name is typed in plain ASCII.

## Mythology

The stories of Belobog place light, good, fortune at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Belobog appears in slavic tradition as light, good, ​fortune. The name's meaning, "White god", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Belobog in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into ​the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Belobog survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does ​not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Belobog gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Zeloboch of the Czech ​Chronicle (The Chronicle Line)

The only medieval author to name Belobog is **Cosmas of Prague**, whose *Chronica Boemorum* (c. 1125, Book I.4) describes the pre-Christian Czechs sacrificing to demons — and lists among ​them *Zeloboch*, the chronicler's Latinized rendering of Belobog, alongside gods of the sky, the harvest, and fortune. The sentence is a sneer from a Christian cleric, and its spelling is garbled; yet it ‌proves that around 1100 a 'White God' received offerings in Bohemia. Cosmas is careful to mock the whole catalogue — sky, harvest, and fortune gods jumbled together — which is exactly why scholars mine ​his scorn for the only list of Czech deities that survives. No myth accompanies the name.No myth accompanies the name. But the attestation does real work: **it converts Belobog from a scholarly inference ‌into a historical god, however thinly witnessed** — one line carrying the whole bright half of Slavic dualism.

### Chernobog at Rethra (The Black God)

Belobog's structure is completed by his opposite. **Helmold of ​Bosau** (*Chronica Slavorum* I.52, c. 1172) reports that the Slavs acknowledged a god of all evil 'whom they call the Black One' — *Chernobog* — and modern scholarship assembles the pair: White God ‌and Black God, light and evil, the Slavic dualism (Gieysztor, *Mitologia Słowian*; Rosik, *Białobóg*). Later folklore strengthens the pairing: across the Slavic world the year's good and ill fortune are personified as opposed ​powers, and the White God's wreath is the benign half of that old bookkeeping. Historians rightly cautionHistorians rightly caution that the two attestations come from different peoples, centuries, and authors — no text ‌shows the pair worshiped together. The dualism is thus partly reconstruction. Still, the reconstruction rests on two independent medieval witnesses: **wherever the sources reach the Slavic gods, they find darkness named — and ​naming darkness implies, at least to us, its bright counterpart**.

### Belobog in the Last Sheaf (The Kept Wreath)

Slavic harvest folklore preserved the god's name as a thing. Across Poland and Russia, the ‌final sheaf of the harvest was shaped into a wreath called **belobog** ('white god') and kept in the house — above the door, by the icons, or in the granary — until the ​spring sowing, when its grain went back into the field to carry the year's fortune forward (records collected in nineteenth-century ethnography; discussed by Gieysztor and Rosik). Ethnographers found the wreath hung beside the ​household icons — a quiet index of how long a pagan guest can lodge in a Christian home without ever being named aloud. The custom binds the White GodThe custom binds the White ‌God to the oldest agricultural contract: **prosperity is a guest that must be housed, fed, and returned**. Whatever his theology, Belobog lived in the rafters of Slavic farmhouses within living memory of the ‌ethnographers.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Belobog concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Belobog, carrying scholarly and ‌cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Light, Good, Fortune

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Belobog across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each ​one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Belobog carries the same precision in textual form.

- **White (Bělъ)** — Light itself — the color-word at the root of his ​name and of Slavic words for dawn and brightness
- **The Harvest Wreath** — The last-sheaf wreath called belobog in Polish and Russian folklore, kept till spring to house the field's fortune
- **The Waxing Light** ‌— The growing half of the year — the season attributed, in folk reconstruction, to his governance
- **The Honored Seat** — The right-hand place at table and hearth — the 'white' side in ​Slavic custom, opposite the unclean left

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Belobog with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for ​a Slavic name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, ‌it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Belobog, sanctuary or cult remains tied to light and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against ​the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Belobog** is light, good, fortune. The name means "White god" and belongs to the slavic tradition.

### Sacred Name

The ​restoration Belobog returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Light

Central domain: light, good, fortune.

### Living Tradition

Honored in slavic myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple despite the ‌unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### The White God

His very name is his office: bělъ, 'white' — light, brightness, and the good they signify.

### Counter of the Black God

He exists in structure as much ​as in story — the bright pole balancing Chernobog's darkness.

### The Chronicle God

'Zeloboch' among the demons of Cosmas of Prague — one line, two words, a whole theology.

## Across Cultures

Within the ‌Slavic tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[dazhbog|Dažbog]], [[lada|Lada]], [[marzanna|Marzanna]], [[morana|Morana]], [[perun|Perun]], and [[radagast|Radagast]].

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Belobog may be likened to figures in neighboring traditions without being identical ​to them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Belobog makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

## Cultural Legacy

Belobog remains a touchstone for understanding slavic ​religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Belobog includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that ​afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Belobog remains findable and citable.

## A Meditation

To contemplate Belobog is to hold the idea ‌of light, Good, Fortune in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "White god" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than ​mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as light, Good, Fortune · White god.

Sit with the restored form — Belobog — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a ‌small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *belobog* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in ​turn.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Belobog add ‌up to a single argument — that a name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. The PuniCodex restoration keeps that record in working order: the temple presents it, the Scholarly Edition footnotes it, ​the lexicon catalogs it, and the domain makes it addressable. *belobog* will always exist as a fallback. But fallback is not identity. **Belobog** is the name; everything else is a convenience.

## A Closer ‌Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Belobog**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name ​in Slavic transcription rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *belobog* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as ​the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, ​the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **b**, **e**, **l**, **o**, **b**, **o**, **g** ‌— so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and ​addressable.

## Belobog in Its Tradition

**Belobog** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Slavic tradition, where it is counted among 21 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Light, Good, Fortune ‌— places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company ​of its kin. When the address bar shows **Belobog**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point ‌of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Belobog** is one such ​vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Belobog** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; ​it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. ​That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *belobog*. Now the public ‌web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding ‌— is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.
